parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the difference between a system left to oscillate freely on its own and a system pushed repeatedly by an outside driver - what two frequencies are involved here?
Hint 2: Remember what happens to the size of the response when those two frequencies match - think about maximum energy transfer and amplitude.
parts.proper_answer: Resonance is oscillation at maximum amplitude when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Two frequencies to compare**
Every oscillating system has its own natural frequency, the frequency it vibrates at when displaced and released with no driver. A forced oscillation has a separate driving frequency from the external periodic force. Resonance is all about the relationship between these two.

Step 2: **The resonance condition**
When you drive the system exactly at its natural frequency, energy is transferred most efficiently on each cycle because the driver is always in step with the motion. The amplitude builds up to a maximum. So resonance means $f_{driving} = f_{natural}$ giving maximum amplitude.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.2 - the peaks get smaller gradually over several oscillations rather than stopping at once. What general process causes free oscillations to die away?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading the decay shape**
In Fig. 4.2 the ball is in free oscillation after release, with no driver. The displacement-time trace is still oscillatory but the envelope of the peaks shrinks slowly with time. That gradual loss of amplitude over many cycles is the signature of damping, and because it lasts for many oscillations it is specifically light damping.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from energy - for a free oscillation with no energy input, what must happen to the total mechanical energy if the amplitude is getting smaller?
Hint 2: Think about what opposes the motion of the ball through air and in the string, and how doing work against that opposition removes energy.
parts.proper_answer: The amplitude decreases because the oscillations lose energy due to work done against resistive forces, such as air resistance and friction at the string, acting on the ball.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Amplitude means energy**
For an oscillator, maximum kinetic energy and elastic potential energy are proportional to (amplitude)$^2$. A smaller amplitude therefore directly means less total mechanical energy remains in the oscillation.

Step 2: **Where the energy goes**
With the generator off there is no input to replace energy. Resistive or dissipative forces such as air drag on the ball and internal friction in the string oppose the velocity and do negative work on every swing. Mechanical energy is transferred to thermal energy of the surroundings, so the amplitude decays with time.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on repeating points on Fig. 4.2, for example successive upward zero crossings or successive peaks, and read off the time for one full cycle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the period from the graph**
Pick the same point in successive cycles. For example upward crossings of zero are near $t \approx 0.07\text{ s}$ and $t \approx 0.32\text{ s}$, or peaks near $0.13\text{ s}$ and $0.38\text{ s}$. The difference is one period: $$T \approx 0.32 - 0.07 \approx 0.25\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Convert to frequency**
Frequency and period are inverses: $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{0.25} = 4.0\text{ Hz}$$ This is the natural frequency of free oscillation of the ball on the string.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Now the generator is driving the ball - recall from (a) at what driving frequency the response should be largest, using your value from (b)(iii).
Hint 2: Picture how amplitude behaves well below and well above that special frequency, so the sketch rises to a single smooth peak and then falls again.
parts.proper_answer: Sketch of amplitude against $f$ starting low, rising to a single sharp maximum at $f = 4.0\text{ Hz}$ and then falling to low values by $10\text{ Hz}$ - the resonance curve.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where the peak must be**
With the driver on, this is forced oscillation. You found the natural frequency is $4.0\text{ Hz}$. By the definition of resonance, amplitude is maximum when $f$ equals the natural frequency, so your curve must peak at $f = 4.0\text{ Hz}$.

Step 2: **Shape of the resonance curve**
Start with small amplitude at $f = 0$. As $f$ increases toward $4.0\text{ Hz}$ the amplitude rises smoothly to a single maximum. As $f$ increases beyond $4.0\text{ Hz}$ toward $10\text{ Hz}$ the driver is out of step and amplitude falls again. Draw one smooth peak only, fairly narrow because damping is light.
